activities.anchor: diverge precisely where elite sport lives
activities.caption: the two curves — drag the divider to the decoupling
activities.name: tasHealthCompare

config.prompt: One athlete, two curves — drag the divider:

before.label: the fitness curve
before.text: periodised upward in blocks — a Tour de France podium finisher in peak fitness can be immunosuppressed and energy-deficient

after.label: the health curve
after.text: protected continuously (sleep, nutrition, monitoring) so the fitness curve can keep climbing — the classic 'overtraining' endgame is where they split

config.why: The monitoring stack exists mostly to detect where the two curves decouple: performance first plateaus, then falls as illness and staleness arrive.

config.prompt: Illness risk plotted against training load — which curve is the lesson's?

curves.label: low at moderate load, high at both extremes

config.why: Sedentary living and extreme training loads both raise illness risk — elite cohorts show elevated upper-respiratory-infection rates during heavy blocks. Managing the trade-off, not ignoring it, is the job.

activities.caption: pair each fuel with its storage-and-delivery profile
activities.name: tasFuelMatch

config.prompt: Match each fuel to its storage-and-delivery profile:

pairs.right: 400–500 g — the limiting fuel; depletion in 60–90 minutes of high-intensity effort is the bonk
tens of thousands of kilocalories even in lean athletes, delivered slowly
1.6–2.2 g per kg of body mass per day — a building-materials budget, not a fuel

config.why: Fuelling decisions are evaluated against measured workloads — kilojoules from power meters, GPS distance — with carbohydrate periodised around sessions and protein distributed across the day.

config.prompt: The classical components — file each one:
config.why: The expert discipline is matching protocol to question — a screening battery, a return-to-play ladder and a research study need different precision, and each extra decimal point costs equipment, time and athlete goodwill.

activities.anchor: in sport where 1% separates the podium
activities.caption: mark the smallest change worth detecting
activities.name: tasSwcPlace

config.prompt: On this scale of observed improvement, place the smallest change an elite test must resolve:
config.why: A test must resolve smaller differences than it would in a physical-education class — most field tests cannot, which is why elite environments repeat tests, average trials and read trends across sessions rather than verdicts from single numbers.

activities.caption: run the audit every test must pass
activities.name: tasWhyBranch

config.root: You are drafting the season's testing calendar. A colleague proposes a new protocol 'because more data never hurts.'

start.text: The proposal sits in the calendar draft. Where do you push back?

choices.label: Ask which decision depends on its result
choices.feedback: That question is the whole audit — testing earns its place by the decisions it serves.

choices.label: Accept it — the squad can never be too measured
choices.feedback: Every test costs training time and attention, and a squad measured weekly on ten protocols learns to perform the test, not the sport.

decision.text: The result routes somewhere: a strength block for the weak jumper, a fuelling plan for the low ferritin, a monitored ramp for the returning player. The test keeps its slot.

theatre.text: No decision depends on the number — it changes nothing in the programme. The slot is freed for training.

config.why: Defensible testing: baseline and profiling, feedback and motivation, return-to-play milestones, talent identification and load prescription. If no decision depends on the result, the test is theatre.

activities.anchor: The analytical era began as market arbitrage
activities.caption: size the data stream one player generates
activities.name: tasGpsEst

config.prompt: GPS units sample at 10 Hz. Roughly how many position fixes does one player log in a 90-minute match?
config.why: Ten fixes every second for 5,400 seconds ≈ 54,000 — the stream behind total distance, high-speed running, sprint counts and accelerometer-derived 'load'.
config.context: Acute-to-chronic workload ratios and similar heuristics read this stream as risk flags for conversation, not injury oracles.

config.prompt: The pre-season battery, assembled in order:
items: State the question: who is ready to train at what intensity, and what does each player need?
Aerobic capacity: the Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test (level 1) — total distance covered
Lower-limb power: countermovement jump on a force platform, with left–right asymmetry from the force trace
Speed: 10-metre (acceleration) and 30-metre (maximal) sprints on timing gates
Repeat-sprint ability: a purpose-built protocol — single sprints miss the fatigue that decides matches
Every result lands with its measurement error attached and routes to a decision
config.why: The battery repeats on a fixed calendar so trends, not snapshots, drive the programme — and few tests, chosen for the decisions they serve, beat many.
